overview.title: Running the JAX training loop; why JAX is different; meet Keras
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.section: 3.5 Introduction to JAX / 3.6 Introduction to Keras
overview.subsection: 3.5.5 What makes the JAX approach unique
overview.main_topic: The final training loop of the pure-JAX linear classifier, a balance sheet of JAX's strengths and frictions, and the opening of the Keras section
overview.central_idea: In JAX, the model state (W, b) lives outside the training step: each call to the jitted, stateless `training_step()` takes the current weights and returns new ones. This functional, stateless design is what enables JAX's speed and scalability, at the price of harder debugging and more verbose low-level loops. With the three low-level frameworks covered, the chapter turns to Keras, the high-level API.
overview.importance: The page closes the comparison of the three low-level frameworks, so it is where you can line up how TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX each handle state. It also introduces Keras, the API used for the rest of the book.

paragraphs.excerpt: The main thing that makes JAX unique among modern machine learning frameworks
paragraphs.what_it_says: JAX's defining trait is its functional, stateless philosophy. It may feel like friction at first, but it is what lets JAX compile to extremely fast code and scale to arbitrarily large models and many devices.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A JAX function cannot secretly read or modify variables. Everything it depends on comes in as an argument, and everything it changes goes out as a return value. Because a function's behaviour depends only on its inputs, JAX can trace it once, hand the traced computation to the XLA compiler, and replicate or shard it across devices without worrying about hidden shared state.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the reason behind the awkward-looking `loss, W, b = training_step(...)` pattern. The friction and the speed have the same cause.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Pure functions are referentially transparent, so a trace is a faithful description of the computation. That makes compilation (`jax.jit`) and transformations such as `grad` and parallel mapping safe. (The last part is beyond the book.)

terminology.meaning: Functions hold no persistent state between calls; outputs depend only on inputs.
Here: tracing the Python function into a computation graph that XLA turns into optimized device code.

connections: p.106: JAX's stateless approach and its benefits for parallel and distributed computation were introduced there.
p.242: the same statelessness makes JAX the most complex backend for low-level Keras training steps.

paragraphs.excerpt: There’s a lot to like about JAX:
paragraphs.what_it_says: There are three upsides. JAX is the fastest framework seen so far for most models. Its numerical API is fully consistent with NumPy. It is the best fit for TPUs, because it was developed from the ground up for XLA and TPUs.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Speed comes from whole-function XLA compilation. NumPy consistency (via `jax.numpy`) means little new API to learn, in contrast to PyTorch's `dim=` vs NumPy's `axis=`. The TPU point reflects history: XLA was created so TensorFlow could run on TPUs, and JAX was built around XLA.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Together these three bullets explain why JAX is popular for large-scale generative AI training (p.106) and why it is a strong Keras backend choice for training speed.

terminology.meaning: Accelerated Linear Algebra, Google's compiler for tensor computations (p.86).
Tensor Processing Unit, Google's specialized deep learning accelerator.

connections: p.98: TensorFlow is called fast but 'JAX is often even faster'.
p.86: history of TPUs and XLA.
p.106: PyTorch's NumPy inconsistencies such as dim vs axis.

paragraphs.excerpt: Using JAX can also come with some amount of developer friction:
paragraphs.what_it_says: There are two downsides. Metaprogramming and compilation make debugging significantly harder than pure eager execution. Low-level training loops are more verbose and harder to write than in TensorFlow or PyTorch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Inside a jitted function, values are abstract tracers during tracing, so a `print` shows a tracer rather than a number, and errors point into traced code. Gradients come from transforming a function (`value_and_grad(compute_loss)`), not from a tape you can step through. Every piece of state must be threaded through arguments and return values by hand, which makes the code longer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the trade-off: you buy speed and scalability with developer ergonomics. It explains the recurring advice to debug with an eager backend and train with JAX (p.115).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Metaprogramming here means writing functions that produce or transform other functions: `jax.grad`, `jax.value_and_grad` and `jax.jit` all take a function and return a new one.

terminology.meaning: Running each operation immediately as Python executes it, so values are concrete and inspectable (PyTorch's default, TensorFlow without tf.function).
Programs that manipulate programs; in JAX, function transformations like grad and jit.

connections: p.113: grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss) is an example of metaprogramming.
p.242: writing a JAX training step in Keras requires stateless_call().

paragraphs.what_it_says: The reader now knows the basics of all three low-level frameworks and can implement a linear classifier from scratch with each. That is a solid foundation, and the next step is the more productive Keras API.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The low-level tour was there to show what is going on underneath. Keras will automate the parts you just wrote by hand: parameter creation, the training loop and gradient updates.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It marks the shift from mechanics to productivity. From here on, most of the book's code is Keras running on one of these backends.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Keras is a Python deep learning API for conveniently defining and training any kind of deep learning model. It was released in March 2015, with v2 in 2017 and v3 in 2023.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Keras is an API layer, not a tensor engine. It defines models and training workflows and delegates the actual numerical work to a backend. Keras 3 (2023) is the version that is multi-backend again, running on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch (p.115).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The dates show that Keras is the oldest of the four frameworks covered in the chapter (p.85).

p.86: Keras originally ran on Theano, then added TensorFlow support.

concepts.name: Stateless (functional) computation
concepts.definition: A programming style where functions keep no persistent state: all inputs come in as arguments and all changed values go out as return values.
concepts.intuition: Like a vending machine that has no memory. You give it the current weights and data, it hands back a loss and new weights, and you have to keep hold of them yourself.
concepts.technical: In JAX, `training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` returns `(loss, W_new, b_new)`. The caller rebinds `W, b` each iteration. Because the function is pure, `jax.jit` can trace it once and compile it with XLA.
concepts.significance: The book says this property is what unlocks JAX's speed and its ability to scale to many devices.
concepts.example: `loss, W, b = training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)` in the loop on this page.
concepts.misconception: Stateless does not mean the model has no parameters. It means the parameters are not stored inside the functions; they are passed in and returned explicitly.

concepts.name: XLA compilation via jax.jit
concepts.definition: Compiling a Python function into optimized device code through the XLA compiler.
concepts.intuition: Instead of interpreting each operation one at a time, the whole step is translated once into a single fast program.
concepts.technical: `@jax.jit` (p.113) traces the function with abstract values on the first call and compiles the trace. Later calls with the same shapes and dtypes reuse the compiled code. The tracing is what makes debugging harder.
concepts.significance: It is the main source of the speed claim on this page.
concepts.example: The 40 loop iterations here all run the same compiled `training_step`.
concepts.misconception: jit does not make arbitrary Python side effects run on every call. Prints and Python-level mutations happen at trace time only.

concepts.name: Custom training loop
concepts.definition: A hand-written loop that repeatedly computes the loss, its gradients and parameter updates.
concepts.intuition: It is what `model.fit()` does for you behind the scenes.
concepts.technical: Here the loop runs 40 full-batch gradient descent steps on the 2-D toy dataset, printing the MSE loss with 4 decimals each step.
concepts.significance: Writing it by hand in three frameworks shows what Keras automates.
concepts.example: `for step in range(40): loss, W, b = training_step(...)`
concepts.misconception: Custom loops are not always better. They are more flexible but more verbose, especially in JAX.

concepts.name: Keras (as a high-level API)
concepts.definition: A deep learning API for Python for defining and training any kind of deep learning model, released March 2015 (v2 2017, v3 2023).
concepts.intuition: It is the prefab building kit, and TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are the raw materials (p.87).
concepts.technical: Keras supplies layers, models, losses, optimizers, metrics and training loops, and delegates tensor math and autodiff to a backend framework (p.115).
concepts.significance: It is the main tool used for the rest of the book.
concepts.example: YouTube recommendation models are built with Keras, according to the page.
concepts.misconception: Keras is not tied only to TensorFlow. Keras 3 runs on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch.

code.title: Initializing W and b and running the JAX training loop
code.original_code:
input_dim = 2
output_dim = 1

W = jax.numpy.array(np.random.uniform(size=(input_dim, output_dim)))
b = jax.numpy.array(np.zeros(shape=(output_dim,)))
state = (W, b)
for step in range(40):
    loss, W, b = training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)
    print(f"Loss at step {step}: {loss:.4f}")
code.what_it_does: Creates the initial parameters of a linear model with 2 inputs and 1 output, then runs 40 gradient descent steps. Each step replaces W and b with the updated values returned by the stateless training_step, and the loss is printed.

line_explanations.explanation: Two input features (the 2-D points of the toy dataset) and one output (a score compared to 0/1 targets).
W, shape (2, 1), drawn uniformly from [0, 1) with NumPy, then converted to a JAX array. JAX's own random API needs explicit keys (p.107–111); NumPy is used here for convenience.
b, shape (1,), initialized to zeros, as a JAX array.
Packs the parameters into a tuple `state`. The loop below does not use this variable; it passes W and b separately, and training_step repacks them as (W, b) for grad_fn.
40 iterations, the same count as the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions of the classifier.
The core of the stateless style: the function receives the current W and b and returns new ones, which are rebound to the same names. Nothing is mutated in place.
Prints the loss. `loss` is a JAX scalar array; the `:.4f` format converts it to a Python float, which blocks until the device has finished computing it.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: `inputs` (shape (2000, 2), float32) and `targets` (shape (2000, 1)) from the dataset built earlier, plus `training_step` from p.113. Outputs: 40 printed loss lines; final trained W (2, 1) and b (1,).
code.algorithm: Full-batch gradient descent with learning rate 0.1 (fixed inside training_step). Each step computes MSE loss and gradients with value_and_grad and applies W ← W − 0.1·∇W, b ← b − 0.1·∇b.
code.theory_link: This is the same mini-batch SGD idea from chapter 2, here with the whole dataset as one batch. The functional form `(params) -> new params` is the stateless philosophy discussed in 3.5.5.
pitfalls: Forgetting to rebind W and b (e.g. writing `loss, _, _ = training_step(...)`) leaves the weights unchanged forever. Nothing is updated in place.
Beyond the book: by default JAX uses 32-bit floats, so the float64 NumPy array is silently cast to float32.
Beyond the book: the first iteration is slower because it triggers tracing and XLA compilation of training_step; later steps reuse the compiled code.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written variant: thread a single state tuple instead of separate W, b
state = (W, b)
for step in range(40):
    loss, *new = training_step(inputs, targets, *state)
    state = tuple(new)
W, b = state

deeper.title: Where the state lives in the three frameworks
deeper.body:
- **TensorFlow** (pp.93–97): `W` and `b` are `tf.Variable`s, updated in place with `assign_sub` inside the training step.
- **PyTorch** (pp.102–105): `W` and `b` are tensors with `requires_grad=True`, updated in place under `torch.no_grad()`, with `.grad` reset each step.
- **JAX** (pp.112–114): `W` and `b` are immutable arrays; `training_step` returns new ones and the loop rebinds the names.

The JAX version is the only one where the training step is a pure function. This is what the book means by 'functional, stateless', and it is why JAX can compile the entire step with no special handling of variables.

deeper.title: Why statelessness helps scaling
deeper.body:
Beyond the book:
1. A pure function's output depends only on its arguments.
2. So the framework can record ('trace') exactly which tensor operations it performs.
3. That trace can be compiled once by XLA into fused, fast kernels.
4. The same trace can be run on many devices at once, each with a shard of the data or parameters, because there is no hidden global variable that devices would have to keep in sync.

This matches the book's statement on p.106 that statelessness 'enables effective automatic parallelization and distributed computation'.

deeper.title: Accounting analogy
deeper.body: PyTorch and TensorFlow are like a shared bank account: the training step reaches in and changes the balance directly. JAX is like a pure calculator. You tell it the current balance and the transactions, it tells you the new balance, and writing that down is your job.

misconceptions.claim: JAX updates W and b in place inside training_step, like TensorFlow's assign_sub.
misconceptions.correction: JAX arrays are immutable. training_step computes new arrays and returns them, and the loop must rebind W and b to them.

misconceptions.claim: The `state = (W, b)` line drives the loop.
misconceptions.correction: As printed, `state` is created but not used in the loop; W and b are passed directly. training_step builds the (W, b) tuple itself for grad_fn.

misconceptions.claim: JAX's statelessness is just an inconvenience.
misconceptions.correction: The book says it is exactly what unlocks fast compiled code and scaling to arbitrarily large models and many devices.

misconceptions.claim: Keras is a separate numerical engine competing with TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
misconceptions.correction: Keras is a high-level API that runs on top of these frameworks as backends (p.87, p.115).

takeaways: In JAX, the training loop rebinds `W, b` to the values returned by a pure `training_step`; nothing is mutated in place.
JAX's functional, stateless philosophy is the source of both its speed and scalability and its friction.
Pros: fastest for most models, NumPy-consistent API, best fit for TPUs and XLA.
Cons: harder to debug than eager execution; more verbose low-level training loops.
Keras is a high-level Python deep learning API (2015; v2 2017; v3 2023) used widely in industry and research.

questions.question: In the JAX loop on this page, why is the line written `loss, W, b = training_step(inputs, targets, W, b)`?
options: Because Python requires functions to return all their arguments
Because training_step is stateless and returns new values of W and b, which must be rebound
Because jax.jit only works on functions with three return values
Because W and b are tf.Variables that must be reassigned
questions.answer: Because training_step is stateless and returns new values of W and b, which must be rebound
questions.explanation: JAX functions don't modify state. The updated parameters are return values (p.113–114). Python imposes no such rule, jit has no return-count requirement, and W and b are JAX arrays, not tf.Variables.

questions.question: Name the three advantages of JAX the authors list.
questions.answer: It's fast (fastest for most models); its numerical API is fully consistent with NumPy; it's the best fit for TPUs since it was built for XLA and TPUs.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets under 'There's a lot to like about JAX'.

questions.question: Explain how the same design choice causes both JAX's speed and its debugging difficulty.
questions.answer: Statelessness plus compilation: pure functions can be traced and compiled by XLA into fast code and distributed across devices. But tracing and compilation (metaprogramming) mean you aren't stepping through concrete eager operations, so debugging is harder.
questions.explanation: The book ties both speed and scaling to the functional, stateless philosophy, and lists metaprogramming and compilation as the cause of debugging friction.

questions.question: What are the shapes of W and b at initialization in this loop?
questions.explanation: W = uniform(size=(input_dim, output_dim)) = (2, 1) and b = zeros((output_dim,)) = (1,). The other options transpose or misread the dimensions.

questions.question: When were Keras v1, v2 and v3 released?
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of section 3.6.

questions.question: Is the variable `state` used by the loop on this page? What does that tell you about how training_step is called?
questions.answer: No. It is created but the loop passes W and b separately; training_step itself packs them into (W, b) when calling grad_fn.
questions.explanation: See the code on this page and the definition of training_step on p.113.

questions.question: Can you describe where the model's parameters 'live' in the TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX versions of the classifier, and how each version updates them?
questions.answer: TensorFlow: tf.Variables updated in place with assign_sub. PyTorch: requires_grad tensors updated in place under no_grad. JAX: immutable arrays returned by the training step and rebound.
questions.explanation: If you can do this, you understand the main difference the chapter has been building toward.
